finding.guards_checked: No authentication, signature, session, or token verification in this code; no auth decorator or middleware; ACL check itself is correct for the identity it receives. Exploitable only if clients can reach the app without a trusted proxy that overwrites the header.

verdict.guard_found: None in the code under review. The only authorization logic is acl.py:5 (is_allowed, a bool) and acl.py:8-10 (ensure_allowed, which aborts with 403). Both are correct for the identity they receive, but views.py:11 takes that identity directly from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header with no signature, session, or token check. views.py:17 and views.py:25 both rely on it, and no auth decorator or middleware exists.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches (views.py:11 reads the header unverified, views.py:17 and :25 gate on it, acl.py:5 and :10 implement the check), and no in-code control blocks spoofing. Whether an attacker can reach this app with a forged header depends on a deployment-side proxy that overwrites or strips the header, and neither that proxy nor any deployment config is in the repo (only views.py and acl.py exist), so reachability cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.guards_checked: None prevent the 500 vs 403 distinction; impact limited to existence disclosure of IDs.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only pre-check is load_user (views.py:9-11), which just reads a header into g.user and does not gate existence. STORE[fid] (views.py:16, 24) is a bare dict lookup that raises KeyError, which Flask turns into a 500. For an existing ID without a grant, is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) returns False, ensure_allowed (acl.py:10) calls abort(403), and rename_file returns an explicit 403 (views.py:25-26). No handler catches the KeyError, so the 500-vs-403 split is reachable.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: views.py:16 and :24 do an unguarded STORE[fid] lookup that yields a 500 for unknown IDs, while acl.py:10 and views.py:26 return 403 for existing IDs without a grant. The endpoints have no authentication gate that prevents this (g.user is just a header value, views.py:11), so any caller who can reach the app can distinguish valid from invalid IDs; the impact is limited to existence disclosure, which matches the low severity claimed.
